claims.text: The abstract introduces SafeWebWorld, a benchmark evaluating safety sufficiency (whether a predictive interface preserves policy-decisive information to separate EXECUTE, ASK, and BLOCK actions) across five web-safety domains via action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions.

In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% were judged semantically plausible, yet several models showed highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour: low false-safe execution, poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases, and a strong preference for BLOCK.
Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate.
Under Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR), frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain.
Within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, so aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour.
